Steller's sea cow (Hydrodamalis gigas) was a colossal sirenian that inhabited the cold waters of the North Pacific. Neonates of this species were remarkably large at birth, with a total length at birth of 318 centimeters [Lb = 318 centimeters], a size that reflects the substantial intrauterine growth period required for this marine mammal. The ultimate total length of fully grown adults reached an impressive 900 centimeters [Li = 900 centimeters], making it one of the largest marine herbivores of its era. At birth, the wet weight of a newborn calf was estimated at 855,000 grams [Wwb = 855,000 grams], a value derived from allometric comparisons with the closely related dugong (Dugong dugon). The ultimate wet weight of a fully mature adult has been calculated at 11,196,000 grams [Wwi = 11,196,000 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase in mass from the neonatal stage. These extreme body dimensions placed Steller's sea cow far outside the typical size range of modern sirenians.

Gestation in Hydrodamalis gigas was a remarkably prolonged affair, with the gestation time estimated at 450 days [tg = 450 days], a duration that aligns with historical accounts from Georg Steller suggesting a pregnancy exceeding one year at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This extended period of foetal development, occurring at a stable body temperature of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C], allowed the calf to attain its already considerable birth dimensions before parturition. Following birth, the calf remained dependent on maternal care for an extensive period; the time since birth at weaning has been inferred at 450 days [tx = 450 days], essentially mirroring the gestation interval at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This parity between gestation and the nursing phase is unusual among large mammals and suggests a life-history strategy heavily invested in the survival of a single, well-provisioned offspring. The thermal regime of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C] underpinned all metabolic and developmental processes, including the energetically expensive lactation period.

Reproduction in Steller's sea cow proceeded at an exceptionally slow pace, consistent with the species' large body size and the constraints of a cold-water herbivorous diet. Evidence suggests that females produced a single calf per event [N_R_i = single calf per event], and that such events occurred approximately once every 5 years [F_R_i = events occurred approximately once every 5 years], given the extended gestation and prolonged maternal care. The low reproductive rate, a consequence of the slow life history, made the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation by human hunters. All reproductive activity and metabolic function were supported by a core body temperature of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C], a value typical for large marine mammals adapted to cold waters.

Sexual maturation in Hydrodamalis gigas was a delayed process, consistent with the extended developmental timeline observed across its life history. The time since birth at puberty was reached at approximately 2,190 days [tp = approximately 2,190 days], equivalent to about 6 years of age, under the species' stable thermal regime of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C]. This lengthy pre-reproductive period allowed individuals to attain the substantial body size and energy reserves necessary to support the demands of gestation and lactation. The onset of gonadal activity at this age marks a significant investment in somatic growth before any reproductive effort is undertaken. This slow maturation pattern is characteristic of K-selected species that occupy stable environments with low predation pressure but face significant energetic constraints related to body size and thermoregulation in cold water. The life span of Hydrodamalis gigas was correspondingly long, with maximum longevity estimated at 36,500 days [am = 36,500 days], or roughly 100 years, a figure extrapolated from the known maximum age of the smaller dugong at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C].

This longevity, when coupled with the protracted time to sexual maturity of about 2,190 days [tp = about 2,190 days] and the extended generational turnover, created a demographic structure highly sensitive to adult mortality at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. The species' low reproductive rate, stemming from a single calf per event and an inter-birth interval of approximately five years, meant that population recovery from even modest levels of exploitation was exceedingly slow. Comparisons with the dugong, a smaller relative with a shorter life span and faster reproductive rate, highlight the extreme end of the slow life-history continuum occupied by Hydrodamalis gigas. All vital rates, from the 36,500-day maximum longevity to the 450-day gestation, were sustained at the species' typical body temperature of 33.0 °C [T = 33.0 °C], a condition that constrained both metabolic rates and the pace of life.
